engine.name: A.R.I.A. Operational Portfolio Engine
engine.purpose: Evaluate the active body of operational work as a portfolio rather than as isolated work items. The engine compares valid obligations, commitments, risks, issues, opportunities, decisions, capacity demand, scheduling constraints, and strategic importance to determine portfolio-level execution posture without overwriting canonical work-item priority or silently discarding lower-ranked obligations.
principles: The portfolio is not merely a sorted task list.
Individual work-item priority remains owned by Priority Engine.
Portfolio reasoning determines how valid work competes for finite execution capacity.
The highest-priority item is not automatically the only work that should receive capacity.
A healthy portfolio protects critical work while still advancing important non-urgent work.
Committed work and speculative opportunity must remain distinguishable.
Portfolio feasibility must reflect practical capacity rather than theoretical availability.
A.R.I.A. should recognize when the total plan cannot be achieved as represented.
Portfolio optimization must not silently cancel, defer, renegotiate, or delegate obligations.
Portfolio recommendations should expose consequential tradeoffs rather than pretend everything can fit.
Portfolio reasoning must remain explainable and provenance-preserving.

rules: Portfolio scope must be explicitly known or reasonably supported.
A.R.I.A. must not compare unrelated work merely because it exists in the same database.
The same work item may participate in multiple legitimate portfolio views.
Portfolio membership does not change ownership of the underlying work item.

healthy.description: Current valid obligations have a plausible execution path within available capacity and supported constraints.

pressured.description: The portfolio remains feasible, but limited capacity, timing, or competing obligations leave reduced flexibility.

constrained.description: Material tradeoffs or adjustments are required to preserve consequential outcomes.

overcommitted.description: Current valid obligations cannot all be satisfied as represented within supported capacity and timing.

unstable.description: Frequent priority, conflict, capacity, issue, or schedule changes prevent a reliable execution posture.

recovery.description: The portfolio is operating under an explicit plan intended to recover from overload, disruption, or accumulated backlog.

unknown.description: Available information is insufficient to determine portfolio health.

requirements: Portfolio records must preserve the underlying work-item identities.
Portfolio classifications must not replace canonical work-item states.
Unknown portfolio values must remain unknown rather than inferred from missing records.
Material portfolio history should remain recoverable.

classes.critical_execution: Consequential actionable work requiring immediate or near-term execution capacity.
classes.committed_execution: Work required to protect supported commitments.
classes.decision_required: Work whose meaningful progression depends on an authorized decision.
classes.issue_recovery: Corrective work associated with active consequential problems.
classes.dependency_wait: Valid work currently awaiting a prerequisite.
classes.delegated_execution: Work actively governed through delegated execution.
classes.protected_progress: Important non-urgent work intentionally protected from starvation.
classes.routine_execution: Valid operational work appropriate for normal execution capacity.
classes.opportunity_consideration: Qualified beneficial potential not yet equivalent to mandatory committed work.
classes.monitoring: Work or conditions requiring observation rather than current execution.
classes.terminal: Resolved work excluded from active execution allocation.

rules: Classification is a portfolio planning view and must not rewrite work_item.type or work_item.status.
One work item may legitimately contribute to more than one portfolio consideration.
Portfolio presentation should avoid unnecessary duplication of the same underlying obligation.

execution_focus.purpose: Determine the limited set of work that should receive active execution capacity during the current planning window.
rules: Execution focus should reflect priority, commitments, timing, dependencies, capacity, context, issues, risks, and strategic importance.
Execution focus must remain smaller than the complete active portfolio when practical.
Not every Priority 1 item necessarily requires simultaneous execution.
Work requiring the user's unique authority should remain distinguishable from work executable by others.
Blocked or legitimately waiting work should not occupy active execution capacity unless useful blocker-removal work exists.
Execution focus should preserve enough capacity for unavoidable operational variation when supported.
Portfolio Engine consumes canonical priority rather than recalculating it.
A portfolio containing many high-priority items may indicate overcommitment, weak priority differentiation, or genuinely exceptional conditions.
Portfolio Engine should not downgrade individual priorities merely to make the distribution appear balanced.
When too many items compete at the same priority level, the engine should evaluate execution sequencing and consequence rather than inventing new priority scores.
Persistent inability to distinguish execution order may require Decision or Conflict evaluation.

anti_starvation.purpose: Ensure legitimate lower-urgency work receives execution opportunity before endless reactive work makes it permanently invisible.
signals: strategic work receives no execution windows
rules: Starvation does not make low-value work more consequential than critical work.
A.R.I.A. should protect execution opportunities for valid chronically displaced work when feasible.
Protected progress should be intentionally scheduled rather than treated as leftover capacity only.
Repeated displacement of protected work should trigger explicit portfolio reassessment.
Obsolete work should be resolved rather than protected merely because it is old.

reactive_load.purpose: Measure how much portfolio capacity is being consumed by unplanned urgent work, active issues, interruptions, and recovery activity.
signals: new urgent work repeatedly displaces planned work
protected work repeatedly lost to reactive conditions
rules: Reactive work may be entirely legitimate.
High reactive load should not be interpreted as poor performance without supporting evidence.
Persistent reactive load may indicate structural capacity, planning, customer, process, or risk conditions.
Portfolio Engine should expose the cost of reactive load on planned work.
Supported commitments should be evaluated against available capacity and execution timing.
Commitment volume should include the work required to fulfill commitments, not merely the number of promises.
A portfolio may be overcommitted even when each individual commitment appeared reasonable when made.
Overcommitment must not silently release or renegotiate any commitment.
Material overcommitment should trigger Capacity, Conflict, Decision, Scheduling, Commitment, and possibly Escalation reevaluation.
Portfolio Engine allocates planning attention to available capacity findings; Capacity Engine owns actual capacity evaluation.
Scarce capacity should preferentially protect higher-consequence obligations while preserving intentional progress on valid non-urgent work where feasible.
Specialized capacity must not be treated as universally interchangeable.
Unused capacity in one dimension does not offset shortage in another unrelated dimension.
A.R.I.A. should expose capacity that is unavailable because of skill, travel, equipment, authority, context, or other supported constraints.

questions: Can all current supported commitments plausibly be satisfied?
Can critical issues receive sufficient corrective capacity?
Can required decisions occur before their useful decision windows close?
Can blocked work be appropriately handled without consuming unusable capacity?
Can strategically important work receive meaningful progress?
Is protected capacity repeatedly being consumed?
Are multiple obligations depending on the same constrained resource?
Does the plan rely on persistent exceptional effort?
Does the schedule have enough practical room for known uncertainty?
rules: A portfolio is not feasible merely because every work item has a due date.
A portfolio is not feasible merely because every work item has been assigned.
A portfolio is not feasible if execution requires impossible sequencing or unsupported capacity.
When the portfolio is infeasible, A.R.I.A. should identify the dominant constraints and required tradeoffs.

current.description: What should receive execution capacity now.

near_term.description: What must be prepared, started, decided, or protected soon.

upcoming.description: Work whose future execution path needs deliberate preparation.

strategic.description: Important work requiring continued progress despite limited immediate urgency.

rules: Planning horizons should remain distinct from canonical priority.
High-priority work may appear in a later horizon when prerequisites legitimately prevent immediate execution.
Strategic work should not disappear merely because it lacks immediate urgency.
Portfolio Engine may recommend tradeoffs but cannot silently execute them.
Consequential tradeoffs requiring authority must be routed through Decision Engine.
Commitment changes must remain governed by Commitment Engine.
Delegation changes must remain governed by Delegation Engine.
Schedule changes must remain governed by Scheduling Engine.
Terminal disposition must remain governed by Resolution Engine.

user_load.purpose: Separate the organization's active portfolio from work that actually requires the user's personal involvement.

categories.user_execution: Work the user must personally execute.
categories.user_decision: Work requiring the user's supported decision authority.
categories.user_review: Work requiring meaningful user review or approval.
categories.user_awareness: Work the user should know about but need not presently act on.
categories.delegated: Work being executed elsewhere under appropriate governance.
categories.quiet: Valid work currently requiring no useful user involvement.

rules: The active organizational portfolio must not be presented as the user's personal task list.
Delegated work should remain governed without consuming unnecessary direct user attention.
A.R.I.A. should aggressively distinguish work requiring the user's unique authority from work that others can handle.
Attention Engine retains authority over actual user-facing presentation.

daily_posture.purpose: Provide a concise operational picture suitable for executive-assistant synthesis.
rules: Daily posture should not dump the complete work inventory on the user.
A.R.I.A. should surface exceptions, consequential changes, and required actions.
Routine healthy work should remain available but quiet.
The portfolio view should answer what the user needs to do, what others are doing, and what is at risk.
Orchestration Engine coordinates individual engine evaluation.
Portfolio Engine evaluates the resulting body of work across multiple work items.
Orchestration may invoke Portfolio Engine after material changes affecting cross-item execution posture.
Portfolio findings may trigger reevaluation of individual work items through their owning engines.
Portfolio Engine must not directly overwrite individual canonical engine states.
Priority Engine owns canonical work-item priority.
Portfolio Engine consumes priority as one input to execution allocation.
Portfolio Engine must not manufacture lower priority merely because capacity is insufficient.
Portfolio sequence and canonical priority must remain distinguishable.
Portfolio Engine determines portfolio-level significance and recommended user load.
Attention Engine determines what actually reaches the user.
Portfolio conditions should normally be consolidated rather than surfaced as dozens of independent notifications.
Portfolio Engine must not independently interrupt the user.
Capacity Engine owns practical capacity evaluation.
Portfolio Engine evaluates how available capacity is allocated across valid work.
Portfolio Engine must not assume missing capacity can be created.
Scheduling Engine owns practical execution timing for work items.
Portfolio Engine evaluates whether schedules collectively form a plausible plan.
Individual feasible schedules may still create an infeasible portfolio when combined.
Portfolio Engine must not independently modify authoritative calendars.
Conflict Engine owns materially incompatible obligations or constraints.
Portfolio Engine may expose cross-item contention requiring Conflict Engine evaluation.
Portfolio infeasibility should not be silently solved by dropping lower-ranked work.
Aging Engine owns aging pressure and starvation detection.
Portfolio Engine uses those findings to protect meaningful progress across the body of work.
Portfolio Engine must not convert age directly into priority.
Opportunity Engine owns opportunity qualification.
Portfolio Engine determines how pursuing qualified opportunities would interact with existing obligations.
Speculative opportunity must not displace committed execution without appropriate authorization.
Resolution Engine owns terminal disposition.
Resolved work should leave active portfolio execution views.
Portfolio pressure is not a legitimate reason to resolve work.
Portfolio reevaluation should use current canonical outputs from owning engines.
The engine should avoid recalculating the entire portfolio for immaterial work-item changes.
Material portfolio changes may trigger Orchestration, Attention, Capacity, Conflict, Decision, Scheduling, Commitment, Delegation, Aging, Escalation, Opportunity, or Resolution reevaluation.

requirements: Portfolio output must preserve underlying work-item identities.
Portfolio execution sequence must remain distinguishable from canonical priority.
Portfolio recommendations must remain distinguishable from authorized actions.
Unknown capacity or feasibility must not be fabricated.
Material portfolio findings must be available to Orchestration and Attention Engines.

guardrails: Do not treat the portfolio as merely a priority-sorted list.
Do not overwrite canonical work-item priority.
Do not silently cancel lower-ranked work.
Do not assume all high-priority work can execute simultaneously.
Do not assume all available personnel or calendar time is interchangeable capacity.
Do not allow urgent incoming work to permanently starve valid important work.
Do not protect obsolete work merely because it is old.
Do not allow speculative opportunity to silently displace committed obligations.
Do not present the entire organizational workload as the user's personal workload.
Do not pretend an infeasible portfolio is feasible.
Do not manufacture capacity to make the plan fit.
Do not bypass Decision Engine for consequential tradeoffs.
Do not bypass Attention Engine for user-facing presentation.
Do not bypass Resolution Engine for terminal disposition.
Do not modify Core reasoning architecture as part of portfolio management.
